notes.definition: Nuclear radiations are used in medicine for the exploration of internal organs (using radioactive tracers) and for the control or destruction of unwanted tissue such as cancer tumours (radiotherapy).
explanation: Nuclear radiation is used in medicine for two main purposes: to explore internal organs, and to control or destroy unwanted tissue. In both cases the benefits must be weighed against the risks, because ionising radiation can damage healthy cells and increase the risk of cancer.

To explore internal organs, a doctor injects or gives a patient a radioactive tracer: a substance containing a radioactive isotope that is carried to the organ being studied. A gamma camera outside the body detects the radiation and builds up an image of where the tracer has collected, showing how well the organ is working. A good tracer emits gamma rays, because gamma can pass out of the body to the detector and is the least ionising, so it causes the least damage on the way. It should have a short half-life (a few hours), long enough for the scan but short enough that it does not keep irradiating the patient. Technetium-99m (half-life about 6 hours) is widely used, and iodine-123 is used to study the thyroid.

To destroy unwanted tissue, radiotherapy uses radiation to kill cancer cells. In external radiotherapy, beams of gamma rays (or high-energy X-rays) are aimed at the tumour from several different directions. The beams overlap only at the tumour, so it receives a large dose while the surrounding healthy tissue receives a much smaller dose. In internal radiotherapy, a radioactive source is placed inside the body next to or inside the tumour. Beta emitters are often used, because beta has a short range in tissue, so the damage is concentrated in the tumour. For example, iodine-131, a beta emitter, is taken up by the thyroid gland and is used to treat thyroid cancer.

Every use of nuclear radiation carries some risk. Radiation can damage DNA in healthy cells, which might cause cancer years later, and high doses can cause radiation sickness. Doctors and patients evaluate perceived risks using data such as the dose in millisieverts and the estimated risk of harm, compared with the benefit of diagnosing or treating a serious illness. A scan that gives a dose similar to a year of background radiation is usually judged worthwhile if it can detect a life-threatening disease.

Hospital staff also take precautions: they keep sources shielded, use tongs, limit their exposure time and wear dosimeters. Patients may be advised to avoid close contact with others, particularly pregnant women and young children, for a short time after receiving a radioactive substance.
keyFacts: Nuclear radiation is used in medicine to explore internal organs and to control or destroy unwanted tissue.
A tracer is a radioactive isotope taken into the body so that its path can be followed.
Tracers should be gamma emitters so the radiation can leave the body and be detected.
Tracers should have a short half-life (hours) to limit the dose to the patient.
Technetium-99m (half-life about 6 hours) is a common tracer.
External radiotherapy: gamma beams from several directions overlap at the tumour.
Internal radiotherapy: a source (often a beta emitter) is placed in or near the tumour.
Iodine-131 is a beta emitter used to treat thyroid cancer.
Benefits must be weighed against risks, using data such as dose (mSv) and risk of harm.

keyTerms.definition: A radioactive isotope taken into the body so that its movement or where it collects can be detected from outside.
A detector placed outside the body that forms an image from gamma rays emitted by a tracer.
Treatment that uses ionising radiation to control or destroy unwanted tissue such as cancer cells.
Radiotherapy using beams of radiation from outside the body aimed at the tumour.
Radiotherapy in which a radioactive source is placed inside the body, next to or inside the tumour.
How dangerous people believe something to be, which may differ from the actual risk shown by data.

workedExamples.title: Tracer activity after a scan
workedExamples.question: A patient is given technetium-99m with an activity of 600 MBq. Its half-life is 6 hours. Calculate the activity 24 hours later.

workedExamples.title: Choosing a tracer
workedExamples.question: Which is the best tracer: P (alpha, 6 hours), Q (gamma, 6 hours), R (gamma, 20 years) or S (beta, 2 minutes)?
steps: Alpha (P) cannot leave the body and is very damaging inside it.
R has too long a half-life: it would irradiate the patient for years.
S decays too quickly to complete a scan, and beta is absorbed by tissue.
Q emits gamma, which leaves the body, and lasts long enough for a scan.

workedExamples.title: Using risk data
workedExamples.question: A scan gives a dose of 5 mSv. The estimated extra risk of developing cancer is 1 in 20 000 for each mSv. Calculate the risk from the scan.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think tracers should be alpha emitters because alpha is easy to stop.
misconceptions.right: In fact alpha cannot get out of the body to be detected, and it is very damaging inside the body. Tracers use gamma emitters.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a tracer should have a long half-life so it lasts a long time.
misconceptions.right: In fact a short half-life (hours) is used, so the patient is not exposed to radiation for longer than needed.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think radiotherapy only damages cancer cells.
misconceptions.right: In fact radiation also damages healthy cells; techniques such as using several beams aim to reduce the dose to healthy tissue.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think patients become permanently radioactive after a scan.
misconceptions.right: In fact the tracer decays (and is excreted) within a day or two because of its short half-life.

realWorld: Technetium-99m scans are used millions of times a year worldwide to check bones, the heart and kidneys.
Radioactive iodine-131 treatment is used to treat an overactive thyroid and thyroid cancer.
Small radioactive seeds implanted in the prostate (brachytherapy) are used to treat prostate cancer.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is in separate Physics (8463) only. It is not assessed in Combined Science Trilogy (8464).
examTips: For tracer questions, justify the choice with two properties: type of radiation (gamma, to leave the body) and half-life (short, but long enough for the test).
For radiotherapy, explain why beams are aimed from different directions: the tumour gets a high dose and healthy tissue a lower dose.
When asked to evaluate risks, use the numbers given, compare with the benefit, and give a conclusion.
Do not confuse tracers (diagnosis, low dose) with radiotherapy (treatment, high dose to kill cells).
summary: Medical uses: exploring internal organs and destroying unwanted tissue.
Tracers: gamma emitters with short half-lives, detected by a gamma camera.
Radiotherapy: gamma beams from several directions, or internal beta sources.
Benefits must be weighed against risks using data such as dose.
Precautions protect both patients and staff.

questions.question: Which type of radiation should a medical tracer emit?
markScheme: 1 mark: Gamma
questions.explanation: Gamma rays can pass out of the body to be detected and are the least ionising. Alpha and beta would be absorbed in the body.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a medical tracer?
markScheme: 1 mark: To explore internal organs
questions.explanation: Tracers are used to explore internal organs and check how they are working. Destroying cancer cells is radiotherapy.

questions.question: What is radiotherapy used for?
options: Destroying unwanted tissue such as tumours
markScheme: 1 mark: Destroying unwanted tissue such as tumours
questions.explanation: Radiotherapy uses radiation to control or destroy unwanted tissue.

questions.question: Which half-life is most suitable for a tracer injected into a patient?
markScheme: 1 mark: 6 hours
questions.explanation: 6 hours gives enough time to do the scan, and the activity then falls quickly. Seconds is too short; years would irradiate the patient for too long.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows how beams of gamma rays are used in external radiotherapy.
Why are the beams aimed at the tumour from several different directions?
options: So the beams cancel out in healthy tissue
So that the tumour gets a high dose while healthy tissue gets a lower dose
Because gamma rays cannot travel in straight lines
markScheme: 1 mark: So that the tumour gets a high dose while healthy tissue gets a lower dose
questions.explanation: Each beam passes through different healthy tissue, but all overlap at the tumour, concentrating the dose there.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a small beta source placed inside a tumour.
Why is a beta emitter often used for internal radiotherapy?

Beta passes straight out of the body

questions.question: Why is an alpha emitter not used as a tracer?
options: Its half-life is always too long
It is not detected by any instrument
It is the most penetrating radiation
It cannot pass out of the body and is very damaging inside it
markScheme: 1 mark: It cannot pass out of the body and is very damaging inside it
questions.explanation: Alpha is absorbed within a few cells, so it would not reach a detector outside the body, and it is strongly ionising.

questions.question: A patient is given a tracer with an activity of 800 MBq and a half-life of 6 hours. What is its activity 18 hours later?
markScheme: 1 mark: 100 MBq
questions.explanation: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 half-lives: 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 MBq. 266 MBq comes from dividing by 3.

questions.question: Iodine-131 is used to treat thyroid cancer. Why is it effective?
options: It emits only gamma rays that pass through the thyroid
It is taken up by the thyroid and emits beta radiation that kills nearby cells
It is an alpha emitter that stays outside the body
It has a half-life of several thousand years
markScheme: 1 mark: It is taken up by the thyroid and emits beta radiation that kills nearby cells
questions.explanation: The thyroid absorbs iodine, so the isotope collects there. Its beta radiation is absorbed by thyroid tissue, killing cancer cells.

questions.question:
A patient is given a dose of technetium-99m with an activity of 480 MBq.
The half-life of technetium-99m is 6 hours.
Calculate the activity after 24 hours.
markScheme: 1 mark: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 half-lives
questions.explanation: Four halvings: 480 → 240 → 120 → 60 → 30 MBq.

questions.question:
A patient is treated with iodine-131 with an activity of 3200 MBq.
Iodine-131 has a half-life of 8 days.
Calculate the time taken for the activity in the patient to fall to 400 MBq.
Assume that no iodine leaves the body.
markScheme: 1 mark: 3200 → 1600 → 800 → 400 is 3 half-lives
1 mark: 3 × 8 = 24 days
questions.explanation: 3200 ÷ 400 = 8 = 2³, so 3 half-lives.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the radiation dose from a CT scan and the average annual background radiation dose in the UK.
Calculate how many years of background radiation give the same dose as the CT scan.
Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.006 Sv = 6 mSv
1 mark: 6 ÷ 2.7 = 2.2 years
questions.explanation: Convert to the same units first: 6 ÷ 2.7 = 2.22, so about 2.2 years.

questions.question:
The extra risk of developing cancer from radiation is estimated to be 1 in 20 000 for each mSv received.
A patient has a scan that gives a dose of 8 mSv.
The risk to the patient can be written as 1 in N.
Calculate the value of N.

A hospital has two possible tracers, X and Y.
Table 1 gives information about the tracers.
Calculate how many times greater the activity of Y is than the activity of X after 8 hours.
markScheme: 1 mark: X: 4 half-lives, 640 ÷ 16 = 40 MBq
1 mark: Y: 1 half-life, 640 ÷ 2 = 320 MBq
1 mark: 320 ÷ 40 = 8 times
questions.explanation: Y decays much more slowly, so it continues to irradiate the patient for longer.

questions.question: Give the two main uses of nuclear radiation in medicine.
markScheme: 1 mark: exploration of internal organs (tracers)
1 mark: control or destruction of unwanted tissue (radiotherapy)
questions.explanation: These are the two uses named in the specification.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a patient who has been given a radioactive tracer.
Device X detects the gamma rays from the tracer inside the patient.
Name device X.
markScheme: 1 mark: gamma camera
questions.explanation: A gamma camera builds up an image from gamma rays leaving the body.

questions.question: Explain why a medical tracer should have a short half-life.
markScheme: 1 mark: its activity falls quickly after the scan
1 mark: so the patient receives a smaller dose / less damage to healthy cells
questions.explanation: Long half-life tracers would keep irradiating the patient after the test.

questions.question: Explain why a tracer must not have a half-life that is too short.
markScheme: 1 mark: it would decay before it reached the organ / before the scan is complete
1 mark: so the activity would be too low to detect / produce an image
questions.explanation: The tracer has to last long enough for the procedure.

questions.question: Describe the risks to a patient of being treated with radiotherapy.
markScheme: 1 mark: radiation can damage (kill) healthy cells as well as cancer cells
1 mark: may cause side effects such as radiation sickness / increased risk of another cancer later
questions.explanation: The aim is to make the benefit greater than these risks.

questions.question:
A patient is worried about having a tracer scan.
Table 1 gives some data about radiation doses.
Suggest how a doctor could use the data in Table 1 to reassure the patient.
markScheme: 1 mark: compare the dose with background radiation (about 2.7 mSv per year, so about 1.5 years' worth)
1 mark: the extra risk of harm is very small (e.g. 1 in 5000)
1 mark: the benefit of diagnosing the illness is greater than the small risk
questions.explanation: Using data helps match perceived risk to actual risk.

rows: Average background dose in the UK each year
Estimated extra risk of cancer for each mSv received

questions.question: Explain why patients who have been given a radioactive tracer are advised to avoid close contact with pregnant women for a day or two.
markScheme: 1 mark: the patient emits gamma radiation, which can irradiate people nearby
1 mark: a developing baby's cells are especially sensitive to radiation damage (and after a day or two the tracer has decayed)
questions.explanation: The short half-life means the advice is only needed briefly.

questions.question: What does a gamma camera produce?
options: An image showing where a tracer has collected
A measurement of the patient's temperature
markScheme: 1 mark: An image showing where a tracer has collected
questions.explanation: The gamma camera detects gamma rays from the tracer and forms an image of the organ.

questions.question: Which property makes technetium-99m a good medical tracer?
options: It emits alpha particles and has a half-life of 6 years
It emits beta particles and has a half-life of 6 seconds
It emits alpha particles and has a half-life of 6 hours
It emits gamma rays and has a half-life of about 6 hours
markScheme: 1 mark: It emits gamma rays and has a half-life of about 6 hours
questions.explanation: Gamma leaves the body to be detected, and a 6-hour half-life is long enough for a scan but short enough to limit the dose.

questions.question: State why ionising radiation can be used to destroy cancer cells.
markScheme: 1 mark: ionising radiation damages (kills) cells / damages their DNA
questions.explanation: The same property that makes radiation hazardous is used to kill unwanted cells.

questions.question: Describe how a radioactive tracer is used to explore an internal organ, and explain the properties the tracer should have.
markScheme: Indicative content: tracer is injected, swallowed or inhaled; carried to and collects in the organ; gamma camera outside body detects radiation and forms image; shows how organ is working or blockages; should emit gamma so radiation passes out of the body and is weakly ionising; short half-life (hours) so dose is low but long enough for the test; e.g. technetium-99m.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear description of the process and both properties explained.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): basic description or one property given.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Both properties (gamma and short half-life) need a reason.

questions.question:
Radiation is used in medicine both to explore internal organs and to destroy cancer tumours.
Compare these two uses, including the type of radiation, the half-life of the sources and the dose involved, and evaluate the risks and benefits to the patient.
markScheme: Indicative content: tracers: gamma emitter so it leaves body; short half-life (hours); low dose; benefit is diagnosis; risk small (small increase in cancer risk); radiotherapy: external gamma beams from several directions overlap at tumour, or internal beta sources placed in/near tumour (short range, damage concentrated), e.g. iodine-131 for thyroid; high dose deliberately to kill cells; risk of damage to healthy tissue, side effects, radiation sickness, later cancers; benefit is treating a life-threatening disease; evaluation: benefits normally outweigh risks, use of data such as dose in mSv; precautions for staff and patients.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed comparison of both uses with correct radiation types, half-lives and doses, and a reasoned evaluation of risks and benefits with a conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes both uses with some correct properties and some evaluation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about one or both uses.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Compare like with like: radiation type, half-life, dose and purpose. Finish with a judgement about benefits versus risks.
